title: Values in variables
summary: The $ sigil, reassignment, dynamic typing, quoting rules, null, and constants.

blocks.html:
A variable is a name for a value. In PHP the name wears a $: $studentName. There is no declaration and no type to write down — a variable exists from the line that first assigns it.

The name itself is letters, digits and underscores, and the first character after the sigil cannot be a digit. The convention for ordinary variables is camelCase; constants use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE.

blocks.title: what a name may look like
blocks.code:
<?php

$studentName = "Maria Santos";   // camelCase, the usual style
$_debugFlag = "prefixed with underscore";
$score2 = 92;

echo $studentName, " / ", $_debugFlag, " / ", $score2, "\n";

// $2fast = "no";   // parse error: a name cannot start with a digit

blocks.html:
= is assignment, not comparison. Assigning to the same name again replaces the value: the old one is simply gone. Nothing declares a type either, so a variable can hold an integer on one line and a string on the next.

That freedom is dynamic typing, and it is why PHP gives you var_dump(): the variable will not tell you what is in it, so ask.

blocks.title: reassignment, and a change of type
blocks.code:
<?php

$course = "PHP";
echo $course, "\n";

$course = "PHP 8.4";   // same name, a new value
echo $course, "\n";

$course = 8.4;         // and now a different type
var_dump($course);

blocks.title: echo shows the value, var_dump shows the type
blocks.code:
<?php

$total = 42;

echo $total, "\n";   // the text only
var_dump($total);    // type and value
var_dump("42");      // same characters, different type

blocks.html: Read that last line as: a string of two characters, containing 42. var_dump() always prints the type first, and for strings it also prints the length. Keep it in one hand while you learn — it reports what PHP stored, not what you assumed.

blocks.title: double quotes read variables, single quotes do not
blocks.code:
<?php

$name = "Juan";

echo "Hello, $name\n";        // double quotes: the variable is replaced
echo 'Hello, $name' . "\n";   // single quotes: the text stays literal
echo "Escaped: \$name\n";     // a backslash keeps the dollar sign

blocks.html: Single quotes are literal all the way down: they do not interpolate $name and they do not understand \n — you get a backslash and an n. Use double quotes when a variable should be replaced, single quotes when the text is just text.

A variable that has never been assigned is not empty — it is undefined, and reading it emits a warning. null is different: it is a real value we assign on purpose to mean nothing yet. isset() answers the question you usually have: does this variable exist and is it not null?

blocks.title: null and isset()
blocks.code:
<?php

$middleName = null;

var_dump($middleName);
var_dump(isset($middleName));   // set, but null: false
var_dump(isset($nickname));     // never assigned: also false

$middleName = "Santos";
var_dump(isset($middleName));   // now true

blocks.html: A constant names a value that must never change. It has no $, it is visible everywhere in the file, and assigning to it is an error. const is the modern form; define() is the function form, which still appears in older code and for names built at runtime.

blocks.title: const and define()
blocks.code:
<?php

const TAX_RATE = 0.12;
define('SITE_NAME', 'Student Directory');

echo SITE_NAME, " charges ", TAX_RATE, " tax\n";
var_dump(TAX_RATE);

quiz.q: Which of these is a valid variable name?
quiz.why: Letters, digits and underscores are allowed, but not as the first character, and the $ is not optional. total without a sigil is a bare word, which PHP treats as a constant.
A value in quotes is a string, so var_dump reports the type and the character count. int(42) would be the dump of the bare number 42.

quiz.q: isset($x) returns false. Which value of $x could cause that?
quiz.why: isset() is false only when the variable is undefined or holds null. Zero and the empty string are set, so it returns true for them — which is why isset() is not an emptiness test.

exercise.brief: Create a variable holding the name Maria and one holding the score 92. Print exactly three lines: the name, the score, then one line that reads Maria scored 92 built from a single double-quoted string.
